rv.q: This revival, by director and choreographer Camille A. Brown, is the most essential production of Shange’s masterwork to date.
Not to get too mystical about it, but this impeccably performed, exquisitely choreographed revival manages the same for many of us out there in the dark.
It pulses and pulses with life, singing a Black girl’s song.
The production, which opens April 20, takes the task of revival seriously — it's a joy to witness.
This production doesn't just honor Shange's work; it amplifies it, finding new frequencies in familiar words.
This rousing revival testifies to the magnitude of her imagination and the unyielding power of the female voice.

The revival of Ntozake Shange’s 1976 for colored girls who have considered suicide/when the rainbow is enuf is stunning in every aspect.

While every performer on stage is remarkable in her own right, the glory of this for colored girls is the way in which the singular women draw strength and power as a group and simultaneously embrace the audience within their big, bright, and beautiful rainbow.
Shange's fantasia of poetry, dance and stories holds a power that's not been weakened either by decades or the loss of a once startling newness.
The women’s exuberance, their togetherness, their loyalty to each other, their love for each other, is sustaining for them and a bracing, life-imparting thing to watch for us.
The sounds of humanity are what pierce through.

It’s not an ideal production, but if you can focus on the words themselves rather than the other stimuli thrown your way, it remains essential, vivid, and affirming.

In some ways, For Colored Girls is showing its age, just a bit; it's hard to imagine a similar work being written today without incorporating issues of gender and sexual identity, for example.
Still, Shange’s text, broken into over two dozen segments, feels utterly authentic both for its time as well as of-the-moment.
The generosity with which the play shares its worlds with the women watching it is its greatest strength.
Shange’s cycle of poetic monologues finds a way to put a rainbow of vibrant color back in what can often be a very bleak world.
Somehow Brown has found a way to keep Shange’s work both mysterious and accessible—quite an accomplishment.
